***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

England\\n\\n**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name \"Pen name\")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan \"Puritan\") clergymen active in [England](./England \"England\") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland \"Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland\"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) \"Thomas Young (1587-1655)\")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England \"Church of England\"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.\\n\\nThe name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) \"Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)\"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder \"Edmund Calamy the Elder\"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen \"Matthew Newcomen\"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow \"William Spurstow\"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall\\'s](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton \"John Milton\") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus\\'s reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)\\n\\nThis response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.\\n\\nMilton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions \"Animadversions\")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus \"Apology for Smectymnuus\")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n1. **Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](./England "England") [Nonconformist](./Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](./John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](./Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](./John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

He was born at [Godmanchester](./Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](./Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](./Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](./Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](./Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](./Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](./Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](./Stephen_Marshall_(minister)#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](./Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](./Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](./William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](./St._Margaret's,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](./Earl_of_Essex's_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](./Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](./Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](./Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](./Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

A moderate [Presbyterian](./Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](./Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](./Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](./English_Restoration "English Restoration").

Works
-----

* [A defence of infant-baptism in answer to two treatises](//archive.org/details/defenceofinfantb00mars "iarchive:defenceofinfantb00mars")

He worked as a contributor on:

* [Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus") (contributor)
* [Shorter Catechism](./Shorter_Catechism "Shorter Catechism") (contributor)

### Sermons

* [A sermon Preached before the Honourable House of Commons, now assembled in Parliament](//archive.org/details/asermonpreached00marsgoog "iarchive:asermonpreached00marsgoog"), at their publike Fast, 17 November 1640. Upon 2 Chron. 15. 2 (1641)
* [The Song of Moses, the Servant of God, and the Song of the Lamb](//archive.org/details/songmosesservan00commgoog "iarchive:songmosesservan00commgoog")(1643)
* [A sacred panegyrick, or, A sermon of thanksgiving, preached to the two Houses of Parliament](//archive.org/details/asacredpanegyri00marsgoog "iarchive:asacredpanegyri00marsgoog")....18 January 1643 (1644)
* On the death of [John Pym](./John_Pym "John Pym") [?] (1643)

Thomas Young (Scottish theologian)

Scottish theologian (d. 1655)

**Thomas Young** (c. 1587–1655) was a [Scottish Presbyterian](./Scottish_Presbyterian "Scottish Presbyterian") minister and theologian, resident in England and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"). He was the major author of the [Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus") group of leading [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") churchmen. He was also Master of [Jesus College, Cambridge](./Jesus_College,_Cambridge "Jesus College, Cambridge"), and is known as the tutor to [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") from the age of about ten.

Life
----

He was born in [Perthshire](./Perthshire "Perthshire"), his father William Young being a vicar. He studied at [St Andrews University](./St_Andrews_University "St Andrews University"), graduating M.A. in 1606. He then moved south to England.[[1]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-1)

In London, from before 1612, he worked as a teaching assistant to [Thomas Gataker](./Thomas_Gataker "Thomas Gataker").[[2]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-2) He tutored Milton, possibly from 1618 to 1620 or 1622,[[3]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-3) and continued to correspond with him.[[4]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-4) He then took a position in [Hamburg](./Hamburg "Hamburg"), as minister to English merchants there, returning to England in 1628. Between 1628 and 1655 Young was vicar at the [church of St Peter and St Mary](./Church_of_St_Peter_and_St_Mary,_Stowmarket "Church of St Peter and St Mary, Stowmarket") in Stowmarket and his portrait hangs on the south wall of the church nave.[[5]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-5)

He was the primary author of the pamphlet *An Answer* signed Smectymnuus, an answer to an anonymous publication defending [episcopacy](./Episcopacy "Episcopacy") and in fact written by [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)"). It sparked off several more publications.

He became a [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") member in 1643, and Master of [Jesus College, Cambridge](./Jesus_College,_Cambridge "Jesus College, Cambridge") in 1644. He was expelled as Master in 1650.[[6]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-6)[[7]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-7)

Works
-----

* *Dies Dominica* (1639)
* *Hope's Incouragement pointed at* (1644)
* *Smectymnuus Redivivus* (1669)

**Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](./England "England") [Nonconformist](./Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](./John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](./Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](./John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

He was born at [Godmanchester](./Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](./Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](./Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](./Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](./Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](./Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](./Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](./Stephen_Marshall_(minister)#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](./Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](./Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](./William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](./St._Margaret's,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](./Earl_of_Essex's_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](./Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](./Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](./Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](./Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

A moderate [Presbyterian](./Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](./Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](./Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](./English_Restoration "English Restoration").

Works
-----

* [A defence of infant-baptism in answer to two treatises](//archive.org/details/defenceofinfantb00mars "iarchive:defenceofinfantb00mars")

He worked as a contributor on:

* [Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus") (contributor)
* [Shorter Catechism](./Shorter_Catechism "Shorter Catechism") (contributor)

### Sermons

* [A sermon Preached before the Honourable House of Commons, now assembled in Parliament](//archive.org/details/asermonpreached00marsgoog "iarchive:asermonpreached00marsgoog"), at their publike Fast, 17 November 1640. Upon 2 Chron. 15. 2 (1641)
* [The Song of Moses, the Servant of God, and the Song of the Lamb](//archive.org/details/songmosesservan00commgoog "iarchive:songmosesservan00commgoog")(1643)
* [A sacred panegyrick, or, A sermon of thanksgiving, preached to the two Houses of Parliament](//archive.org/details/asacredpanegyri00marsgoog "iarchive:asacredpanegyri00marsgoog")....18 January 1643 (1644)
* On the death of [John Pym](./John_Pym "John Pym") [?] (1643)

Thomas Young (Scottish theologian)

Scottish theologian (d. 1655)

**Thomas Young** (c. 1587–1655) was a [Scottish Presbyterian](./Scottish_Presbyterian "Scottish Presbyterian") minister and theologian, resident in England and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"). He was the major author of the [Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus") group of leading [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") churchmen. He was also Master of [Jesus College, Cambridge](./Jesus_College,_Cambridge "Jesus College, Cambridge"), and is known as the tutor to [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") from the age of about ten.

Life
----

He was born in [Perthshire](./Perthshire "Perthshire"), his father William Young being a vicar. He studied at [St Andrews University](./St_Andrews_University "St Andrews University"), graduating M.A. in 1606. He then moved south to England.[[1]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-1)

In London, from before 1612, he worked as a teaching assistant to [Thomas Gataker](./Thomas_Gataker "Thomas Gataker").[[2]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-2) He tutored Milton, possibly from 1618 to 1620 or 1622,[[3]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-3) and continued to correspond with him.[[4]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-4) He then took a position in [Hamburg](./Hamburg "Hamburg"), as minister to English merchants there, returning to England in 1628. Between 1628 and 1655 Young was vicar at the [church of St Peter and St Mary](./Church_of_St_Peter_and_St_Mary,_Stowmarket "Church of St Peter and St Mary, Stowmarket") in Stowmarket and his portrait hangs on the south wall of the church nave.[[5]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-5)

He was the primary author of the pamphlet *An Answer* signed Smectymnuus, an answer to an anonymous publication defending [episcopacy](./Episcopacy "Episcopacy") and in fact written by [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)"). It sparked off several more publications.

He became a [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") member in 1643, and Master of [Jesus College, Cambridge](./Jesus_College,_Cambridge "Jesus College, Cambridge") in 1644. He was expelled as Master in 1650.[[6]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-6)[[7]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-7)

Works
-----

* *Dies Dominica* (1639)
* *Hope's Incouragement pointed at* (1644)
* *Smectymnuus Redivivus* (1669)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

**Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](./England "England") [Nonconformist](./Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](./John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](./Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](./John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

He was born at [Godmanchester](./Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](./Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](./Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](./Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](./Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](./Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](./Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](./Stephen_Marshall_(minister)#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](./Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](./Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](./William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](./St._Margaret's,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](./Earl_of_Essex's_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](./Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](./Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](./Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](./Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

A moderate [Presbyterian](./Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](./Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](./Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](./English_Restoration "English Restoration").

Thomas Young (Scottish theologian)

Scottish theologian (d. 1655)

**Thomas Young** (c. 1587–1655) was a [Scottish Presbyterian](./Scottish_Presbyterian "Scottish Presbyterian") minister and theologian, resident in England and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"). He was the major author of the [Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus") group of leading [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") churchmen. He was also Master of [Jesus College, Cambridge](./Jesus_College,_Cambridge "Jesus College, Cambridge"), and is known as the tutor to [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") from the age of about ten.

Life
----

He was born in [Perthshire](./Perthshire "Perthshire"), his father William Young being a vicar. He studied at [St Andrews University](./St_Andrews_University "St Andrews University"), graduating M.A. in 1606. He then moved south to England.[[1]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-1)

In London, from before 1612, he worked as a teaching assistant to [Thomas Gataker](./Thomas_Gataker "Thomas Gataker").[[2]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-2) He tutored Milton, possibly from 1618 to 1620 or 1622,[[3]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-3) and continued to correspond with him.[[4]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-4) He then took a position in [Hamburg](./Hamburg "Hamburg"), as minister to English merchants there, returning to England in 1628. Between 1628 and 1655 Young was vicar at the [church of St Peter and St Mary](./Church_of_St_Peter_and_St_Mary,_Stowmarket "Church of St Peter and St Mary, Stowmarket") in Stowmarket and his portrait hangs on the south wall of the church nave.[[5]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-5)

He was the primary author of the pamphlet *An Answer* signed Smectymnuus, an answer to an anonymous publication defending [episcopacy](./Episcopacy "Episcopacy") and in fact written by [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)"). It sparked off several more publications.

He became a [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") member in 1643, and Master of [Jesus College, Cambridge](./Jesus_College,_Cambridge "Jesus College, Cambridge") in 1644. He was expelled as Master in 1650.[[6]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-6)[[7]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-7)

Works
-----

* *Dies Dominica* (1639)
* *Hope's Incouragement pointed at* (1644)
* *Smectymnuus Redivivus* (1669)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

**Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](./England "England") [Nonconformist](./Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](./John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](./Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](./John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

He was born at [Godmanchester](./Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](./Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](./Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](./Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](./Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](./Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](./Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](./Stephen_Marshall_(minister)#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](./Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](./Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](./William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](./St._Margaret's,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](./Earl_of_Essex's_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](./Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](./Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](./Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](./Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

A moderate [Presbyterian](./Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](./Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](./Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](./English_Restoration "English Restoration").

Thomas Young (Scottish theologian)

Scottish theologian (d. 1655)

**Thomas Young** (c. 1587–1655) was a [Scottish Presbyterian](./Scottish_Presbyterian "Scottish Presbyterian") minister and theologian, resident in England and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"). He was the major author of the [Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus") group of leading [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") churchmen. He was also Master of [Jesus College, Cambridge](./Jesus_College,_Cambridge "Jesus College, Cambridge"), and is known as the tutor to [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") from the age of about ten.

Life
----

He was born in [Perthshire](./Perthshire "Perthshire"), his father William Young being a vicar. He studied at [St Andrews University](./St_Andrews_University "St Andrews University"), graduating M.A. in 1606. He then moved south to England.[[1]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-1)

In London, from before 1612, he worked as a teaching assistant to [Thomas Gataker](./Thomas_Gataker "Thomas Gataker").[[2]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-2) He tutored Milton, possibly from 1618 to 1620 or 1622,[[3]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-3) and continued to correspond with him.[[4]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-4) He then took a position in [Hamburg](./Hamburg "Hamburg"), as minister to English merchants there, returning to England in 1628. Between 1628 and 1655 Young was vicar at the [church of St Peter and St Mary](./Church_of_St_Peter_and_St_Mary,_Stowmarket "Church of St Peter and St Mary, Stowmarket") in Stowmarket and his portrait hangs on the south wall of the church nave.[[5]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-5)

He was the primary author of the pamphlet *An Answer* signed Smectymnuus, an answer to an anonymous publication defending [episcopacy](./Episcopacy "Episcopacy") and in fact written by [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)"). It sparked off several more publications.

He became a [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") member in 1643, and Master of [Jesus College, Cambridge](./Jesus_College,_Cambridge "Jesus College, Cambridge") in 1644. He was expelled as Master in 1650.[[6]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-6)[[7]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-7)

Works
-----

* *Dies Dominica* (1639)
* *Hope's Incouragement pointed at* (1644)
* *Smectymnuus Redivivus* (1669)

and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call\\'d regenerate reason\".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:\\n\\n> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; England\\n\\n**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name \"Pen name\")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan \"Puritan\") clergymen active in [England](./England \"England\") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland \"Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland\"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) \"Thomas Young (1587-1655)\")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England \"Church of England\"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.\\n\\nThe name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) \"Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)\"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder \"Edmund Calamy the Elder\"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen \"Matthew Newcomen\"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow \"William Spurstow\"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall\\'s](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton \"John Milton\") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus\\'s reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)\\n\\nThis response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.\\n\\nMilton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions \"Animadversions\")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus \"Apology for Smectymnuus\")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n1. Please help to [improve](./Wikipedia:WikiProject_Reliability \"Wikipedia:WikiProject Reliability\") this article by [introducing](./Wikipedia:When_to_cite \"Wikipedia:When to cite\") more precise citations. *(February 2012)* *([Learn how and when to remove this message](./Help:Maintenance_template_removal \"Help:Maintenance template removal\"))* |  *([Learn how and when to remove this message](./Help:Maintenance_template_removal \"Help:Maintenance template removal\"))* |\\n\\n**Stephen Marshall** (c.\\u20091594 – 1655) was an [English](./England \"England\") [Nonconformist](./Nonconformist_(Protestantism) \"Nonconformist (Protestantism)\") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](./John_Pym \"John Pym\") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only \"systematic\" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](./Infant_Baptism \"Infant Baptism\")*, against [John Tombes](./John_Tombes \"John Tombes\") (1646).\\n\\nEarly life\\n----------\\n\\nHe was born at [Godmanchester](./Godmanchester \"Godmanchester\") in [Huntingdonshire](./Huntingdonshire \"Huntingdonshire\"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](./Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge \"Emmanuel College, Cambridge\") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](./Wethersfield,_Essex \"Wethersfield, Essex\") in [Essex](./Essex,_England \"Essex, England\"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](./Finchingfield \"Finchingfield\"). In 1636 he was reported for \"want of conformity.\"\\n\\nCivil War years\\n---------------\\n\\nMarshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](./Robert_Baillie \"Robert Baillie\") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](./Stephen_Marshall_(minister)#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](./Short_Parliament \"Short Parliament\") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](./Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon \"Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon\") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](./William_Laud \"William Laud\") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret\\'s, Westminster](./St._Margaret\\'s,_Westminster \"St. Margaret\\'s, Westminster\"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.\\n\\nHe had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex\\'s regiment](./Earl_of_Essex\\'s_regiment \"Earl of Essex\\'s regiment\") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](./Scotland \"Scotland\") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](./Uxbridge_Conference \"Uxbridge Conference\") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter\\'s execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England \"Charles I of England\") at [Holmby House](./Holmby_House \"Holmby House\") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](./Carisbrooke_Castle \"Carisbrooke Castle\").\\n\\nLater life\\n----------\\n\\nA moderate [Presbyterian](./Presbyterian \"Presbyterian\"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](./Westminster_Shorter_Catechism \"Westminster Shorter Catechism\") in 1647, and was one of the \"Triers\" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](./Westminster_Abbey \"Westminster Abbey\"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](./English_Restoration \"English Restoration\").\\n\\nWorks\\n-----\\n\\n* [A defence of infant-baptism in answer to two treatises](//archive.org/details/defenceofinfantb00mars \"iarchive:defenceofinfantb00mars\")\\n\\nHe worked as a contributor on:\\n\\n* [Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\") (contributor)\\n* [Shorter Catechism](./Shorter_Catechism \"Shorter Catechism\") (contributor)\\n\\n### Sermons\\n\\n* [A sermon Preached before the Honourable House of Commons, now assembled in Parliament](//archive.org/details/asermonpreached00marsgoog \"iarchive:asermonpreached00marsgoog\"), at their publike Fast, 17 November 1640. Young (Scottish theologian)\\n\\nScottish theologian (d. 1655)\\n\\n**Thomas Young** (c. 1587–1655) was a [Scottish Presbyterian](./Scottish_Presbyterian \"Scottish Presbyterian\") minister and theologian, resident in England and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\"). He was the major author of the [Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\") group of leading [Puritan](./Puritan \"Puritan\") churchmen. He was also Master of [Jesus College, Cambridge](./Jesus_College,_Cambridge \"Jesus College, Cambridge\"), and is known as the tutor to [John Milton](./John_Milton \"John Milton\") from the age of about ten.\\n\\nLife\\n----\\n\\nHe was born in [Perthshire](./Perthshire \"Perthshire\"), his father William Young being a vicar. He studied at [St Andrews University](./St_Andrews_University \"St Andrews University\"), graduating M.A. in 1606. He then moved south to England.[[1]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-1)\\n\\nIn London, from before 1612, he worked as a teaching assistant to [Thomas Gataker](./Thomas_Gataker \"Thomas Gataker\").[[2]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-2) He tutored Milton, possibly from 1618 to 1620 or 1622,[[3]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-3) and continued to correspond with him.[[4]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-4) He then took a position in [Hamburg](./Hamburg \"Hamburg\"), as minister to English merchants there, returning to England in 1628. Between 1628 and 1655 Young was vicar at the [church of St Peter and St Mary](./Church_of_St_Peter_and_St_Mary,_Stowmarket \"Church of St Peter and St Mary, Stowmarket\") in Stowmarket and his portrait hangs on the south wall of the church nave.[[5]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-5)\\n\\nHe was the primary author of the pamphlet *An Answer* signed Smectymnuus, an answer to an anonymous publication defending [episcopacy](./Episcopacy \"Episcopacy\") and in fact written by [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\"). It sparked off several more publications.\\n\\nHe became a [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\") member in 1643, and Master of [Jesus College, Cambridge](./Jesus_College,_Cambridge \"Jesus College, Cambridge\") in 1644. He was expelled as Master in 1650.[[6]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-6)[[7]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-7)\\n\\nWorks\\n-----\\n\\n* *Dies Dominica* (1639)\\n* *Hope\\'s Incouragement pointed at* (1644)\\n* *Smectymnuus Redivivus* (1669)\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n1. Status Code: 200

Content:
Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

**Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](./England "England") [Nonconformist](./Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](./John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](./Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](./John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

He was born at [Godmanchester](./Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](./Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](./Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](./Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](./Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](./Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](./Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](./Stephen_Marshall_(minister)#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](./Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](./Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](./William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](./St._Margaret's,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](./Earl_of_Essex's_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](./Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](./Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](./Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](./Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

A moderate [Presbyterian](./Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](./Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](./Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](./English_Restoration "English Restoration").

Thomas Young (Scottish theologian)

Scottish theologian (d. 1655)

**Thomas Young** (c. 1587–1655) was a [Scottish Presbyterian](./Scottish_Presbyterian "Scottish Presbyterian") minister and theologian, resident in England and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"). He was the major author of the [Smectymnuus](./Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus") group of leading [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") churchmen. He was also Master of [Jesus College, Cambridge](./Jesus_College,_Cambridge "Jesus College, Cambridge"), and is known as the tutor to [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") from the age of about ten.

Life
----

He was born in [Perthshire](./Perthshire "Perthshire"), his father William Young being a vicar. He studied at [St Andrews University](./St_Andrews_University "St Andrews University"), graduating M.A. in 1606. He then moved south to England.[[1]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-1)

In London, from before 1612, he worked as a teaching assistant to [Thomas Gataker](./Thomas_Gataker "Thomas Gataker").[[2]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-2) He tutored Milton, possibly from 1618 to 1620 or 1622,[[3]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-3) and continued to correspond with him.[[4]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-4) He then took a position in [Hamburg](./Hamburg "Hamburg"), as minister to English merchants there, returning to England in 1628. Between 1628 and 1655 Young was vicar at the [church of St Peter and St Mary](./Church_of_St_Peter_and_St_Mary,_Stowmarket "Church of St Peter and St Mary, Stowmarket") in Stowmarket and his portrait hangs on the south wall of the church nave.[[5]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-5)

He was the primary author of the pamphlet *An Answer* signed Smectymnuus, an answer to an anonymous publication defending [episcopacy](./Episcopacy "Episcopacy") and in fact written by [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)"). It sparked off several more publications.

He became a [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") member in 1643, and Master of [Jesus College, Cambridge](./Jesus_College,_Cambridge "Jesus College, Cambridge") in 1644. He was expelled as Master in 1650.[[6]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-6)[[7]](./Thomas_Young_(Scottish_theologian)#cite_note-7)

Works
-----

* *Dies Dominica* (1639)
* *Hope's Incouragement pointed at* (1644)
* *Smectymnuus Redivivus* (1669)
